sources.cite: IETF RFC 9846, The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3 (July 2026), section 4.5.1 Certificate
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through summarizing fetches: 'The sender's certificate MUST come in the first CertificateEntry in the list'; 'Each following certificate SHOULD directly certify the one immediately preceding it'; 'a certificate that specifies a trust anchor MAY be omitted from the chain'. So the server sends its leaf and the intermediate that signed it; the client already holds the root.

The company, partner, times and cutoff are invented teaching values; api.example.com is a documentation domain. Command output is an authored rendering in openssl's style. That browsers often succeed anyway because they cache or fetch missing intermediates while many server-side clients do not is common behavior stated as the author's, not read on a page for this round.

brief.situation: You are on call for the API edge at a fictional payments marketplace. At 22:00 the team renewed the TLS certificate for api.example.com. Browsers are fine, but since 22:05 the partner Northwind Pay's callback client refuses to connect: 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. Callbacks not delivered by midnight settle a day late. It is 23:10.
handover: The CA delivered three files: leaf.pem, intermediate.pem and fullchain.pem (leaf then intermediate).
The partner's engineer offers to switch certificate verification off on their side to get callbacks moving.
howItWorks: Pick a command or a change from the action list. Nothing you pick is typed or executed: every step shows an authored result.
Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The cutoff runs on the same clock.
When you close the incident you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident review: why the partner could not verify us, what you changed, and how you know.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Trust is a chain: the leaf is signed by an intermediate, which is signed by a root the client trusts. The server sent only the leaf; clients that do not fetch or cache intermediates cannot build the path. Not a missing root and not a bad certificate.
parts.modelAnswer: Depth 0 only: the intermediate was not sent.

parts.label: What you changed
parts.criteria: Serve the leaf followed by the intermediate (the root may be omitted). Leaf plus root still lacks the link; switching verification off removes authentication of the server, which is what the certificate is for; last year's certificate only buys two days.

parts.label: How you know
parts.criteria: After the reload, s_client with only the system trust store returns 0 and the partner's test callback verifies the chain.

fixed.headline: Good: send the missing link
fixed.body: A certificate proves a key belongs to a name only through a chain of signatures up to a root the client trusts. The server sent the leaf alone; browsers filled the gap, the partner could not. Sending the intermediate fixed every client, and verification stayed on.

fixedGaps.headline: Working, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: Callbacks flow, but on a certificate two days from expiry, or the fix went in without looking at the chain or proving it with a clean trust store.

stillFailing.headline: Still untrusted
stillFailing.body: The root is not missing; the client already trusts it. The intermediate that links the leaf to the root is what the server must send.

insecure.headline: Verification switched off
insecure.body: Turning off verification removes the only proof the partner has that it is talking to you. Fix the chain instead.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was recorded before the case's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: A TLS client trusts a server's certificate when it can follow signatures from the leaf up to a root it already trusts. The new leaf was issued by an intermediate, and nginx served leaf.pem alone; browsers cache or fetch intermediates, so they were fine, while the partner's Java client could not build the path (verify error 20). TLS 1.3 has the server send its own certificate first, each next certificate certifying the one before, and lets it omit the root. Serve fullchain.pem (leaf then intermediate), reload, and prove it with a clean trust store and the partner's test call. Switching the partner's verification off defeats the purpose of the certificate; last year's chain only buys two days.
